tagline: A prisoner's letter of thanks and joy to his most faithful church, centered on the Christ who emptied himself and was exalted.
overview:
Philippians is Paul's warmest letter. He writes from prison, facing a trial that could end in his death, to a church that had supported him from the beginning and had just sent him a gift by the hand of one of their own members, Epaphroditus. He thanks them, tells them how his imprisonment has actually spread the gospel, and urges them to stand together, to put others' interests ahead of their own, and to keep rejoicing in the Lord whatever their circumstances.

At the heart of the letter stands a passage many scholars think was an early Christian hymn (2:6-11). It tells how Christ Jesus, existing in the form of God, did not hold on to his equality with God but emptied himself, took the form of a servant, became human, and was obedient to death on a cross, and how God therefore exalted him and gave him the name above every name. Paul holds this up as the pattern of the mind believers are to share. The rest of the letter echoes it: Timothy and Epaphroditus are commended because they live this way, and Paul describes counting his own impressive credentials as loss for the sake of knowing Christ (3:4-11).

The letter is short, personal, and practical, and it contains some of the most loved lines in the New Testament: “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (1:21), “Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice!” (4:4), and “I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength” (4:13), which in context is a statement about contentment in hunger and plenty.
author:
Paul wrote Philippians, with Timothy named alongside him in the greeting (1:1). This is one of the letters nearly all scholars, critical and traditional alike, accept as Paul's own. The personal details, the style, and the theology all fit him, and the letter was known and valued by the early church; Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna in the early second century, wrote his own letter to the Philippians and mentions that Paul had written to them.

The main debate concerns the letter's unity rather than its author. At 3:1 Paul writes “Finally, my brothers”, and at 3:2 the tone turns sharply to warning against opponents, which leads some scholars to think Philippians combines two or three shorter letters of Paul, perhaps including a separate note of thanks for the gift (4:10-20). Many others argue the letter is a single whole, pointing to shared vocabulary and themes that run through every section and noting that Paul often uses “finally” to mark a turn rather than an ending.
date: The date depends on where Paul was imprisoned, and there are three main views. The traditional view places him in Rome, under the house arrest described in Acts 28, around AD 60 to 62. The mention of the palace guard (the praetorium, 1:13) and of believers in the household of Caesar (4:22) fits Rome naturally, and Paul's uncertainty about whether he will live or die fits a trial before the emperor. A second view places him in Ephesus around AD 54 to 55. Acts does not record an imprisonment there, but Paul speaks of many imprisonments (2 Corinthians 11:23) and of great danger in Asia, and Ephesus is much closer to Philippi, which would make the several trips implied in the letter (news of Paul's imprisonment, Epaphroditus's arrival, news of his illness reaching home, and his planned return) easier to explain. A third view places him in Caesarea, where he was held for two years around AD 57 to 59 in Herod's praetorium (Acts 23:35). Each has defenders; the Roman setting remains the most widely held, and the letter's message is the same on any of them.
setting:
Philippi lay in Macedonia, in what is now northern Greece, on the Via Egnatia, the Roman road that ran across the Balkans. It was founded in the fourth century BC by Philip II of Macedon, the father of Alexander the Great, and named after him. In 42 BC, on the plain outside the city, Mark Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius, the assassins of Julius Caesar. Afterward, and again after Octavian's victory at Actium in 31 BC, the city was refounded as a Roman colony and settled with veterans of the Roman army.

As a colony, Philippi was a small piece of Rome planted abroad. Its citizens held Roman citizenship, it was governed by Roman law and Roman magistrates, Latin was prominent in its official life, and its people were proud of their status. That background gives force to Paul's language: he tells the believers to conduct themselves (literally, to live as citizens) in a manner worthy of the gospel (1:27), and reminds them that their citizenship is in heaven (3:20). Acts 16 describes the founding of the church around AD 49 to 50 on Paul's second missionary trip: the conversion of Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, at a place of prayer by the river; the freeing of a slave girl from a spirit of divination; the beating and imprisonment of Paul and Silas; and the conversion of the jailer and his household. The church that began there went on to support Paul financially again and again (4:15-16), and faced opposition of its own (1:28-30).
purpose: Paul writes for several reasons at once. He thanks the Philippians for their gift and their long partnership in the gospel (1:3-5; 4:10-20). He reports on his circumstances and reassures them that his chains have advanced the gospel (1:12-26). He sends Epaphroditus home after a near-fatal illness, explaining why and asking the church to honor him (2:25-30), and plans to send Timothy soon (2:19-24). He urges unity and humility in a church where some members, including two women who had labored with him, Euodia and Syntyche, were at odds (2:1-4; 4:2-3). And he warns them against teachers who would put confidence in circumcision and the flesh, and against those who live as enemies of the cross (3:2-21).
story: Philippians belongs to the period after Acts 16 to 20, when Paul's churches in Macedonia and Greece were growing and he himself was increasingly in chains. It is one of the four Prison Letters, alongside Ephesians, Colossians, and Philemon. In the larger story of the Bible it shows the gospel reaching Europe and a Roman colony, and it shows a church learning to live as citizens of heaven while still inside the empire. Its central hymn draws on Isaiah's picture of every knee bowing to the Lord (Isaiah 45:23) and on the servant of the Lord who is humbled and then exalted, and it looks forward to the day of Christ, when the Savior will come from heaven and transform the bodies of his people (3:20-21).
christ: Philippians contains one of the most important statements about Christ in the New Testament. In 2:6-11, Christ Jesus exists in the form of God and has equality with God, yet he empties himself by taking the form of a servant and being made in human likeness, humbles himself to death on a cross, and is exalted by God and given the name above all names, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. The church's confession that Christ is truly God and truly human, and that he came down to save and was raised and exalted, is written plainly here. Christ is also the one Paul lives for (1:21), the one whose righteousness he receives by faith (3:9), whose sufferings and resurrection he wants to share (3:10), and whose return he awaits (3:20-21).
reading: Read Philippians as a real letter between friends, full of thanks, news, and practical requests. Watch for its key words: joy and rejoicing, the gospel, partnership (koinonia), mind or attitude (the same verb recurs through the letter), and the day of Christ. Notice how the Christ hymn in chapter 2 shapes what follows: Timothy, Epaphroditus, and Paul himself are all shown living out its pattern. Joy in this letter is not cheerfulness or denial; it sits beside chains, rivalry, illness, and the possibility of death. A common misreading lifts single verses such as 4:13 out of context and turns them into promises of success; in context they describe the strength to be content in need as well as in plenty.

structure.title: Greeting, thanks, and prayer
structure.summary: Paul greets the church, thanks God for their partnership in the gospel, and prays that their love will grow in knowledge and discernment.

structure.title: Paul's circumstances
structure.summary: His imprisonment has advanced the gospel; he rejoices that Christ is preached and weighs life and death, confident he will remain for their sake.

structure.title: A life worthy of the gospel
structure.summary: Stand firm together, look to others' interests, and share the mind of Christ, who emptied himself and was exalted; work out salvation and shine as lights.

structure.title: Timothy and Epaphroditus
structure.summary: Paul plans to send Timothy and sends Epaphroditus home, commending both as examples of self-giving service.

structure.title: Knowing Christ
structure.summary: Paul warns against confidence in the flesh, counts his credentials as loss to gain Christ, presses on toward the goal, and points to citizenship in heaven.

structure.title: Final appeals and thanks
structure.summary: Paul urges unity, joy, prayer instead of anxiety, and right thinking, thanks the church for its gift, and closes with greetings.

themes.title: Joy
themes.body: Words for joy and rejoicing appear more than a dozen times in this short letter, written by a man in chains. Paul's joy rests not on circumstances but on the Lord, on the progress of the gospel, and on his friendship with the Philippians. He rejoices that Christ is preached even by rivals (1:18), and he calls the church to rejoice in the Lord always (4:4). This is joy that has looked at suffering and death and not been undone by them.

themes.title: The mind of Christ
themes.body: The letter repeatedly uses a Greek verb meaning to think, to set one's mind, or to hold an attitude. Paul asks the church to be like-minded (2:2) and to have among themselves the mind that was in Christ Jesus (2:5), who did not grasp his status but emptied himself for others. Humility here is not low self-esteem but the free choice to use one's position for the good of others, as Christ did.

themes.title: Partnership in the gospel
themes.body: Paul thanks the Philippians for their partnership (koinonia, a word for shared life and common cause) from the first day (1:5). They prayed, they gave, and they sent one of their own to serve him. Philippians shows the Christian life as shared work in a common mission, not a private spirituality.

themes.title: Citizenship and conduct
themes.body: In a Roman colony proud of its citizenship, Paul tells believers to live as citizens worthy of the gospel (1:27) and reminds them that their citizenship is in heaven (3:20). Their primary loyalty lies with the Lord Jesus Christ, whose coming they await, and that loyalty shapes how they live in Philippi.

themes.title: Suffering and hope
themes.body: Paul writes from prison, the church faces opposition, and Epaphroditus nearly died. The letter does not hide any of this. It sees suffering for Christ as a gift granted to believers (1:29), a sharing in Christ's sufferings (3:10), and it sets all of it within the hope of resurrection and the day of Christ.

keyChapters.why: Paul's thanksgiving and prayer, his report that chains have advanced the gospel, and his reflection that to live is Christ and to die is gain.
The Christ hymn (2:6-11), one of the central passages of the New Testament on who Christ is, set within a call to humility and unity.
Paul counts his own righteousness as loss in order to gain Christ and the righteousness that comes from God through faith.
Calls to rejoice, to pray instead of worrying, and to learn contentment, with Paul's thanks for the church's gift.
